title: Marrero's banjo, resonator and banjo mutes
summary: Marrero used a standard Vega with resonator and head guard; talk turns to banjo mutes, including a leg-operated lever.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Anything else about John Marrero's style? What kind of a banjo did he use?
Well, he used the standard vega them days. You see, the vega was...
Did he have a resonator in those days?

Oh, yes, it had a resonator. It had a resonator and an armrest and a head guard. Most of you see plenty of banjos today. The guy don't have no head guard on them. But that little piece covered the head. You know, when you hit with the pick that kept the head from getting black or something like that.

By the way, Lawrence showed me his banjo a couple years ago. He had a mute on it, too. I forget how Lawrence is... Yeah. Some sort of a mute. Yeah. Somebody else has one. McLean. I think you use your knee or push something.
Lawrence is a different type. Oh, yeah.

You see, some screw on the back of the bridge. Some screw is right on the string and you pull it right to the bridge. And they give it a muted sound. That's what Lawrence said. But there was a banjo that came out called a silver bell bacon.
And that bacon had what you call some kind of a... Well, it was a... It was a mute, but it was...

Yeah, a lever. That's right. It was a lever that was worked by the leg. When it was down, you had a clear tone. When you wanted the muted sound, you brought up your leg and squeezed the lever against the banjo. That's what it was.
